```{r}
#| label: setup

## Run the analysis: the master script creates all tables (tab) and figures (fig) in memory
source("Gambia-NFI-2026-master.R")

library(knitr)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "–")


## Table formatting ####

## Column labels for display
col_labels <- c(
  forest_type = "Forest type", region = "Region", n_pp = "Plots (n)", land_cover = "Land cover",
  area_ha = "Area (ha)", area_mep = "Area ME (%)", area_pct = "Share of country (%)",
  species = "Species", genus = "Genus", family = "Family", taxon_level = "Taxon level",
  density = "Density (trees/ha)", density_ha = "Density (trees/ha)", density_mep = "Density ME (%)",
  basal_area = "Basal area (m²/ha)", n_sections = "Sections (n)",
  rel_density = "Rel. density (%)", rel_frequency = "Rel. frequency (%)", rel_dominance = "Rel. dominance (%)", ivi = "IVI",
  H = "Shannon H'", H_me = "H' ME", H_mep = "H' ME (%)", richness = "Richness", evenness = "Evenness",
  tree_species_name = "Species", tree_family = "Family", tree_iucn_code = "IUCN", tree_iucn_category = "IUCN category",
  n_trees = "Trees (n)", n_plots = "Plots with record (n)", n_plots_total = "Accessible plots (n)", pct_plots = "Plots with record (%)",
  wildlife_type_label = "Wildlife type", wildlife_sign_label = "Type of sign",
  healthy_ha = "Healthy (trees/ha)", healthy_mep = "Healthy ME (%)", damaged_ha = "Damaged (trees/ha)", damaged_mep = "Damaged ME (%)",
  pct_healthy = "Healthy (%)", ratio_healthy_damaged = "Healthy / damaged",
  tree_condition_overall_label = "Condition", pct = "Share of trees (%)",
  disturbance_group = "Group", disturbance = "Disturbance",
  dbh_class = "DBH class (cm)", height_class = "Height class (m)",
  agb_ha = "AGB (t/ha)", agb_ha_mep = "AGB ME (%)", agb_tot = "Total AGB (t)", agb_tot_mep = "Total AGB ME (%)"
)

## Reporting levels: names in tab, subsection titles and cross-reference label suffixes
level_info <- tibble(
  level  = c("country", "forest_type", "forest_type_region"),
  title  = c("Country level", "Forest type level", "Forest type and region level"),
  suffix = c("country", "ftype", "ftype-region")
)

## Format a table for display: remove the columns constant at the level and the columns in .drop,
## readable column names
fmt_tab <- function(.df, .level = NULL, .drop = NULL) {
  if (identical(.level, "country")) .df <- select(.df, -any_of(c("forest_type", "region")))
  if (identical(.level, "forest_type")) .df <- select(.df, -any_of("region"))
  .df <- .df |>
    select(-any_of(.drop)) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.character))
  names(.df) <- coalesce(col_labels[names(.df)], names(.df))
  .df
}

## Print a table with caption and cross-reference label (chunk option results: asis)
print_tab <- function(.df, .caption, .label) {
  cat(kable(.df, format = "pipe", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n: ", .caption, " {#", .label, "}\n\n", sep = "")
}

## One subsection per reporting level with its table (chunk option results: asis).
## Labels: tbl-<id>-country, tbl-<id>-ftype, tbl-<id>-ftype-region
print_levels <- function(.tabs, .id, .caption, .heading = "####", .drop = NULL) {
  pwalk(level_info, \(level, title, suffix) {
    cat(.heading, " ", title, "\n\n", sep = "")
    print_tab(
      fmt_tab(.tabs[[level]], level, .drop),
      .caption = paste0(.caption, ", ", tolower(title)),
      .label = paste0("tbl-", .id, "-", suffix)
    )
  })
}
```

# Methods

## Sampling design and estimation

The NFI follows a two-phase design, also called double sampling for stratification [@cochran1977, chapter 12]:

- **Phase 1** is a systematic grid of `r nrow(ph1_data)` points over the whole country, interpreted on high-resolution imagery in Collect Earth Online (CEO). The grid itself is not stratified: each point is classified after selection into one of four strata (closed forest, open forest, mangrove forest and non-forest). The share of grid points in each stratum estimates the weight, and so the area, of each stratum.
- **Phase 2** is a subsample of the phase 1 points, selected within each forest stratum and visited in the field as clusters of plots. The stratification is therefore only used to select phase 2. Phase 2 provides the tree measurements and the land use and land cover (LULC) observed on the ground.

The stratum areas are not known in advance, as they would be with a wall-to-wall map: they are estimated from the phase 1 grid, and their sampling error is part of the uncertainty of the results (Step 10).

The strata and the reporting domains are two different classifications:

- The **stratum** $h$ is the phase 1 class. It is part of the design and is never changed after selection, even when the field crew observes a different land cover. Each cluster keeps the stratum it was selected in.
- The **domain** $d$ is the forest type observed in the field (closed, open and mangrove forest, and non-forest). Estimates are reported by domain.

Phase 2 corrects the phase 1 classification through the share of each domain within each stratum. For example, part of the area classified as closed forest in phase 1 is found to be open forest or non-forest in the field. That area, and the biomass measured on it, is attributed to the domain observed on the ground, and weighted by the stratum it was selected in.

The estimation follows the steps below.

### Step 1: Phase 1 stratum weights and areas

With $N'$ phase 1 points in the country and $N'_h$ points classified in stratum $h$:

$$W_h = \frac{N'_h}{N'}, \qquad A_h = A \, W_h$$

where $A$ is the land area of the country (ha) and $A_h$ the estimated area of stratum $h$. The weights $W_h$ are computed over all strata, including strata without phase 2 clusters, so that they sum to 1.

### Step 2: Phase 2 selection

In each forest stratum, $n_h$ phase 1 points are selected as phase 2 cluster centres. Clusters are the primary sampling units (PSU). They have 5 plots, or 3 plots in mangrove forest, which are the secondary sampling units. The non-forest stratum is not sampled in phase 2 (see Step 9).

### Step 3: Tree level

Each tree $k$ gets an expansion factor $EF_k$ from the nested plot design:

$$EF_k =
\begin{cases}
1 / 0.04 & \text{if } 10 \le D_k < 20 \text{ cm (20 × 20 m plot)} \\
1 / 0.1  & \text{if } D_k \ge 20 \text{ cm (20 × 50 m plot)}
\end{cases}$$

The tree attribute $y_k$ is, for example, aboveground biomass (t) from @chave2014, using the tree height $H_k$. Missing heights are predicted with a local height-diameter model, a Curtis model with forest type fixed effects and cluster random effects, the form selected for Sudanian savanna woodlands by @valbuena2016.

### Step 4: Plot level

For plot $j$ of cluster $i$, with measured area $a_{ij}$ (0.1 ha when accessible, 0 when not accessible):

$$y_{ijd} = a_{ij} \sum_{k \in (ij, d)} y_k \, EF_k, \qquad x_{ijd} = a_{ij} \sum_{s \in (ij, d)} p_{ijs}$$

- $y_{ijd}$ is the plot total of the attribute for the part of the plot in domain $d$. Each tree is recorded in the LULC section $s$ it stands in. The expansion factors scale the small trees of the 0.04 ha subplot up to the full plot.
- $x_{ijd}$ is the plot area in domain $d$, where $p_{ijs}$ is the area share of LULC section $s$ recorded in the field. A plot that overlaps several forest types is split between domains. When the recorded percentages of a plot do not add up to 100%, they are rescaled to 100%. Accessible plots without a LULC record are treated as non-forest.

### Step 5: Cluster level

Plot values are summed within each cluster:

$$y_{id} = \sum_j y_{ijd}, \qquad x_{id} = \sum_j x_{ijd}, \qquad a_i = \sum_j a_{ij}$$

### Step 6: Within-stratum estimates

For each stratum $h$ and domain $d$, the per-hectare value and the domain share are ratios of sums over the $n_h$ clusters:

$$\bar{y}_{hd} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_h} y_{id}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_h} a_i}, \qquad
\bar{x}_{hd} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_h} x_{id}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_h} a_i}$$

$\bar{x}_{hd}$ is the share of stratum $h$ found in domain $d$ in the field. It is the phase 2 correction of the phase 1 strata. $\bar{y}_{hd}$ is the amount of the attribute in domain $d$ per hectare of stratum $h$.

### Step 7: Combining strata

The stratum estimates are weighted by the phase 1 weights:

$$\bar{Y}_d = \sum_h W_h \, \bar{y}_{hd}, \qquad \bar{X}_d = \sum_h W_h \, \bar{x}_{hd}$$

$\bar{X}_d$ is the share of the country in domain $d$, and $\bar{Y}_d$ the attribute in domain $d$ per hectare of country.

Steps 6 and 7 are equivalent to giving each cluster $i$ of stratum $h$ an expansion weight, the area it represents, $w_i = A_h / \sum_{i=1}^{n_h} a_i$ (ha of country per ha of plot measured in stratum $h$). Domain totals are then weighted sums over all clusters, $\hat{Y}_d = \sum_i w_i \, y_{id}$ and $\hat{A}_d = \sum_i w_i \, x_{id}$. Clusters of strata with fewer phase 2 clusters relative to their phase 1 area carry a larger weight.

### Step 8: Domain estimates

The per-hectare value in domain $d$ is a ratio estimator, and the domain area and total follow from it:

$$\hat{R}_d = \frac{\bar{Y}_d}{\bar{X}_d}, \qquad
\hat{A}_d = A \, \bar{X}_d, \qquad
\hat{Y}_d = A \, \bar{Y}_d = \hat{R}_d \, \hat{A}_d$$

For example, $\hat{R}_d$ is the aboveground biomass of closed forest in t/ha, $\hat{A}_d$ the area of closed forest in ha, and $\hat{Y}_d$ its total biomass in t.

### Step 9: Strata without phase 2 sample

The non-forest stratum has no phase 2 clusters. Each of its phase 1 points is added as a virtual plot, accessible and measured as non-forest with no trees, so for this stratum $\bar{x}_{hd} = 1$ for the Non-forest domain, 0 for the forest domains, and $\bar{y}_{hd} = 0$. The domain areas then add up to the country area. This assumes the non-forest stratum contains no forest and no biomass. It covers about 60% of the phase 1 points, so trees outside forest and forest patches missed in phase 1 are not included in the estimates. Visiting a subsample of non-forest points in future cycles would remove this assumption.

### Step 10: Variance

Within stratum $h$, the variance between clusters of the ratio $\bar{y}_{hd}$ is:

$$s^2_{y,hd} = \frac{1}{n_h - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_h} \frac{\left( y_{id} - \bar{y}_{hd} \, a_i \right)^2}{\bar{a}_h^2},
\qquad \bar{a}_h = \frac{1}{n_h} \sum_{i=1}^{n_h} a_i$$

The variance of $\bar{Y}_d$ combines the phase 2 sampling error within strata and the phase 1 error in the stratum weights:

$$v(\bar{Y}_d) = \sum_h \left[
W_h \, \frac{N'_h - 1}{N' - 1} \, \frac{s^2_{y,hd}}{n_h}
+ \frac{W_h}{N' - 1} \left( \bar{y}_{hd} - \bar{Y}_d \right)^2
\right]$$

$v(\bar{X}_d)$ and the covariance $c(\bar{X}_d, \bar{Y}_d)$ are computed in the same way, replacing $y$ with $x$, and the squares with products of the $x$ and $y$ terms. The variance of the ratio is then:

$$v(\hat{R}_d) = \frac{v(\bar{Y}_d) + \hat{R}_d^2 \, v(\bar{X}_d) - 2 \hat{R}_d \, c(\bar{X}_d, \bar{Y}_d)}{\bar{X}_d^2}$$

and $v(\hat{A}_d) = A^2 \, v(\bar{X}_d)$, $v(\hat{Y}_d) = A^2 \, v(\bar{Y}_d)$.

### Step 11: Confidence intervals

Uncertainty is reported as the margin of error at the 90% confidence level, in absolute terms and as a percentage of the estimate:

$$ME_d = t_{1 - \alpha/2, \; n - H} \, \sqrt{v(\hat{R}_d)}, \qquad
U_d = \frac{ME_d}{\hat{R}_d} \times 100$$

with $\alpha = 0.1$, $n = \sum_h n_h$ the number of accessible phase 2 field clusters and $H$ the number of strata with field clusters. The virtual plots of Step 9 are not counted in $n$ and $H$.

### Assumptions

- **Inaccessible plots** have $a_{ij} = 0$ and are left out of both the numerator and the denominator of the ratios. This assumes that, within a stratum, they are similar to the accessible plots.
- **Trees outside the live tree allometry** (stumps, dead standing trees, and mangroves, palms and baobabs with their own equations) need their own attribute values, which are then added to $y_{ijd}$ in Step 4. Until then, their biomass is not included.

# Results and Discussion

Results are given at three levels: the whole country, each forest type, and each forest type within each administrative region. Forest types are those observed in the field, and plots that cover several forest types are split between them (see Methods).

- **ME** is the margin of error at the 90% confidence level, as a percentage of the estimate. It is not given for domains with a single plot.
- **Plots (n)** is the number of phase 2 clusters with at least one plot section in the domain. In the non-forest domain, it includes the phase 1 points of the non-forest stratum.
- Plot counts (threatened species, wildlife, disturbance) use the accessible field plots, assigned to the forest type of their main LULC section.
- At forest type and region level, many domains have few plots and the estimates are indicative only.

## Biological Diversity

### Tree Species Composition and Diversity

<!-- IVI, Shannon index keep the top 10 or 20. We can do it by species and genus and family -->

The Importance Value Index (IVI) is the sum of the relative density, relative frequency and relative dominance (basal area) of each taxon, from 0 to 300. Density and basal area are two-phase estimates. Frequency is the number of plot sections where the taxon is recorded. Unidentified trees are not included.

The most important species at country level are shown in @fig-ivi-species and @tbl-ivi-species-country, and in each forest type in @fig-ivi-species-ftype and @tbl-ivi-species-ftype. Genera and families are in @tbl-ivi-genus-country to @tbl-ivi-family-ftype-region, and the Shannon index in @tbl-shannon-country to @tbl-shannon-ftype-region and @fig-shannon.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ivi-species
#| fig-cap: "Top 20 species by Importance Value Index, country level."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.8
fig$b_ivi_species
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ivi-species-ftype
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 species by Importance Value Index in each forest type."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 8.5
fig$b_ivi_species_ftype
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-shannon
#| fig-cap: "Shannon index of tree species by forest type and region. Error bars: 90% confidence interval."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
```


#### Shannon diversity index

The Shannon index $H'$ is computed from the estimated density of each taxon in the domain, at species, genus and family level. Richness is the number of taxa recorded, and evenness is $H' / \ln(\text{richness})$.

```{r}
#| results: asis
print_levels(tab$b_shannon, "shannon", "Shannon diversity index", .heading = "#####")
```

### Rare, Threatened and Endangered Tree Species

<!-- Check the whole species list against the IUCN checklist. -->

Tree species are matched with the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (version published on GBIF, `r format(file.mtime("data-anci/iucn/taxon.txt"), "%B %Y")`). Threatened species are in the categories Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN) and Vulnerable (VU). Occurrence is the number of accessible field plots with at least one live tree of the species (@fig-iucn and @tbl-iucn-country to @tbl-iucn-ftype-region). The category of all recorded species is in @tbl-iucn-all.

### Forest Biomass and Carbon Stocks

Aboveground biomass (AGB) of live trees is estimated with the allometric equation of @chave2014. AGB per hectare is the ratio estimate of the domain, and the total AGB is the AGB per hectare times the domain area. At country level, AGB is `r tab$i_biomass$country$agb_ha` t/ha (@tbl-biomass-country), and by forest type and region in @tbl-biomass-ftype, @tbl-biomass-ftype-region and @fig-biomass.

```{r}
#| label: fig-biomass
#| fig-cap: "Aboveground biomass by forest type and region. Error bars: 90% confidence interval, n = number of plots."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
fig$i_biomass
```

```{r}

print_levels(tab$i_biomass, "biomass", "Aboveground biomass")
```
